items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: An economist randomly selected 600 warehouse workers from all warehouse workers employed in a certain state. For each worker, the economist recorded whether the worker had completed a forklift safety certification and what the worker earned per hour. On average, the workers who had completed the certification earned higher hourly wages than the workers who had not.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Completing the certification causes higher hourly wages for warehouse workers in the state.
Completing the certification causes higher hourly wages, but only for the 600 workers in the sample.
Completing the certification is associated with higher hourly wages for warehouse workers in the state.
Completing the certification is associated with higher hourly wages, but only for the 600 workers in the sample.
items.explanation: The economist only recorded what the workers had already done, and nobody was randomly assigned to complete the certification. That means you can claim an association but not a cause. The workers were randomly selected from all warehouse workers in the state, so you can apply the association to that whole population.

A.why: You took a clear wage gap as proof of cause. Nobody was randomly assigned to get certified, though. Workers who chose the course may differ in experience or motivation, so this observational study can't show cause.

B.why: You mixed up the two kinds of randomness. Narrowing the claim to the sample doesn't make a causal claim acceptable, because cause needs random assignment and this study had none.

D.why: You correctly stopped at association but missed that the 600 workers were randomly selected from every warehouse worker in the state. Random selection is what lets you generalize the result to the state.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: A materials engineer took 80 steel bars from a single production batch. The engineer randomly assigned 40 of the bars to receive a new anti-corrosion coating and the other 40 to receive the standard coating. After 30 days in a salt-spray chamber, the bars with the new coating showed significantly less rust than the bars with the standard coating.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The new coating causes less rusting than the standard coating for steel bars like those tested.
The new coating causes less rusting than the standard coating for steel bars from any manufacturer.
The new coating is associated with less rusting, but the study cannot show that the coating causes it.
No conclusion about cause is possible, because the bars were not randomly selected from all steel bars.
items.explanation: The bars were randomly assigned to the two coatings, so you can conclude that the new coating caused the difference in rust. The bars all came from one batch and were not randomly selected from a wider population, so the conclusion only covers bars like the ones tested.

B.why: You got the cause right but stretched it too far. All 80 bars came from one batch, so nothing in the study lets you generalize to steel from any manufacturer.

C.why: You missed the random assignment. When subjects are randomly assigned to treatments, you are allowed to make a cause-and-effect claim, so 'association only' is too weak.

D.why: You mixed up the two kinds of randomness. Random selection controls how far you can generalize, not whether you can claim a cause. Random assignment allows the causal claim, and this study had it.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: An agronomist randomly selected 120 plots from all wheat fields in a certain county. Of these plots, 60 were randomly assigned to receive a new nitrogen fertilizer, and the other 60 received no fertilizer. At harvest, the plots that received the fertilizer had a substantially higher mean yield than the plots that did not.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The fertilizer is linked to higher yields in the county's wheat fields, but it cannot be shown to cause them.
The fertilizer causes higher yields in the 120 plots studied, but this cannot be extended to the county.
The fertilizer causes higher yields in wheat fields in this county and in wheat fields in every other county.
The fertilizer causes higher yields in wheat fields throughout the county from which the plots were chosen.
items.explanation: This study used both kinds of randomness. Random assignment to fertilizer or no fertilizer lets you claim a cause. Random selection from all the county's wheat fields lets you generalize to the county. Only this choice gets both parts right.

A.why: You missed that the plots were randomly assigned to receive the fertilizer. With random assignment, a cause-and-effect conclusion is allowed, not just an association.

B.why: You missed that the plots were randomly selected from all wheat fields in the county. That random selection lets you extend the result to the whole county.

C.why: You generalized past the population that was sampled. The plots came only from this county, so the study says nothing about other counties.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: A hydrologist asked residents of a river valley to volunteer their private wells for testing, and 45 well owners agreed. For each well, the hydrologist measured the distance from the well to the river and the nitrate concentration in the well's water. Wells closer to the river tended to have lower nitrate concentrations.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: For the 45 wells tested, being closer to the river causes lower nitrate concentrations.
For the 45 wells tested, being closer to the river is associated with lower nitrate concentrations.
For all wells in the valley, being closer to the river is associated with lower nitrate concentrations.
For all wells in the valley, being closer to the river causes lower nitrate concentrations.
items.explanation: The hydrologist only measured wells as they already were, and nothing was randomly assigned, so you can only claim an association. The wells were volunteered rather than randomly selected, so the association applies only to the 45 wells tested.

A.why: You accepted a causal claim from an observational study. Nothing was randomly assigned, and other factors such as soil type or nearby farming could explain the pattern.

C.why: You generalized from a volunteer sample. Owners who chose to have their wells tested may not represent the valley, so the result can't be extended to all wells there.

D.why: You made both mistakes. You claimed cause without random assignment, and you generalized to the valley without random selection.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: A city's transportation department identified 40 intersections where residents had complained about speeding. The department randomly assigned 20 of these intersections to have a raised crosswalk installed, and the other 20 were left unchanged. Six months later, the average driving speed had fallen by much more at the intersections with raised crosswalks.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Raised crosswalks cause lower driving speeds at every intersection in the city, including those without complaints.
Raised crosswalks are associated with lower driving speeds, but the study cannot show that they cause them.
Raised crosswalks cause lower driving speeds at intersections similar to the 40 included in the study.
Falling driving speeds caused the department to install raised crosswalks at 20 of the 40 intersections.
items.explanation: The intersections were randomly assigned to get a raised crosswalk or not, so you can conclude that the crosswalks caused the drop in speed. The 40 intersections were chosen because of complaints, not randomly selected, so the conclusion only covers intersections like them.

A.why: You generalized beyond the intersections that were studied. Only intersections with speeding complaints were included, so the study can't speak for every intersection in the city.

B.why: You missed the random assignment. Because chance decided which intersections got crosswalks, a cause-and-effect claim is justified.

D.why: You reversed cause and effect. The crosswalks were assigned at random before speeds were measured, so falling speeds couldn't have decided where they went.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: An immunologist randomly selected 1,000 adults from a registry of all adult residents of a certain city. For each adult, the immunologist recorded the average number of hours the adult slept per night and measured the level of a certain antibody in the adult's blood. Adults who slept more hours per night tended to have higher antibody levels.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Among adults in the city, sleeping more hours is associated with higher antibody levels.
Among adults in the city, sleeping more hours causes higher antibody levels.
Among adults in every city, sleeping more hours causes higher antibody levels.
Only among the 1,000 adults sampled is sleeping more associated with higher antibody levels.
items.explanation: The immunologist recorded how much people already slept and didn't assign sleep amounts, so you can claim only an association. The adults were randomly selected from all adults in the city, so the association applies to the city's adults.

C.why: You made two errors. You claimed cause without random assignment, and you generalized to every city when the sample came from one city only.

D.why: You missed that the 1,000 adults were randomly selected from all adults in the city. Random selection lets you extend the association to that whole population.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: A meteorologist reviewed one year of records from 50 weather stations that had been chosen for a regional monitoring network. For each night, the meteorologist compared the amount of cloud cover with the overnight low temperature. At these stations, nights with more cloud cover tended to have higher overnight low temperatures.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: At these 50 stations, more cloud cover causes higher overnight low temperatures.
At these 50 stations, more cloud cover is associated with higher overnight low temperatures.
At these 50 stations, higher overnight low temperatures cause more cloud cover.
At weather stations worldwide, more cloud cover is associated with higher overnight lows.
items.explanation: The meteorologist only looked at existing records, and nothing was randomly assigned, so you can claim an association but not a cause. The stations were chosen for a regional network rather than randomly selected from stations worldwide, so the conclusion is limited to these 50 stations.

C.why: You reversed the direction and still made a causal claim. Observational records can't support a cause in either direction.

D.why: You generalized beyond the stations studied. They were picked for one regional network, not randomly selected from stations around the world.

Linen fragments that yellow less are more likely to be stored in acid-free boxes.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: Researchers randomly selected 300 patients aged 65 or older from the registry of a hospital network. Half of these patients were randomly assigned to receive a high-dose flu vaccine, and the other half received the standard dose. One month later, the high-dose group had significantly higher average antibody levels than the standard-dose group.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The high dose causes higher antibody levels for the network's patients aged 65 or older.
The high dose causes higher antibody levels for the network's patients of every age group.
The high dose is associated with higher antibody levels, but it cannot be said to cause them.
The high dose causes higher antibody levels for the 300 patients studied and for no one else.
items.explanation: The dose was randomly assigned, so you can conclude cause and effect. The patients were randomly selected from the network's patients aged 65 or older, so the conclusion applies to that group.

B.why: You generalized past the population that was sampled. Only patients aged 65 or older were selected, so the result says nothing about younger patients.

C.why: You treated this experiment like an observational study. Randomly assigning the dose is exactly what allows a causal conclusion.

D.why: You overlooked the random selection. The 300 patients were randomly drawn from the network's older patients, so the conclusion extends to that whole group.

items.stimulus: A coach recruited 40 college swimmers who volunteered for a training study. items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The tapering plan causes greater improvement for all college swimmers.
The tapering plan is associated with greater improvement for all college swimmers.
The tapering plan is associated with greater improvement for the swimmers studied.
The tapering plan causes greater improvement for swimmers like those studied.
items.explanation: The swimmers were randomly assigned to tapering or usual training, so you can conclude that the plan caused the greater improvement. They volunteered rather than being randomly selected, so the conclusion is limited to swimmers like those in the study.

C.why: You stopped at association even though the plan was randomly assigned. Random assignment is what allows a cause-and-effect conclusion.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: A printmaking instructor recruited 60 volunteers from her weekend relief-printing workshops. She randomly assigned 30 of them to ink their blocks with a new rolling technique and the other 30 to use the standard technique. items.stem: Which of the following is an appropriate conclusion?
choices: The new technique causes more even ink coverage for printmakers in general.
The new technique causes more even ink coverage for workshop volunteers like these.
The new technique is associated with more even ink coverage, but it is not shown to cause it.
The new technique is associated with more even ink coverage for printmakers in general.
items.explanation: First ask about random assignment: the instructor randomly assigned volunteers to the two techniques, so you can conclude that the technique caused the difference. Then ask about random selection: the 60 people were volunteers from her own workshops, not a random sample of all printmakers. So the causal conclusion only applies to people like those in the study.

A.why: You were right that random assignment lets you claim cause, but you stretched the result to all printmakers. The subjects were workshop volunteers, not randomly selected from all printmakers, so you can't generalize that far.

D.why: You mixed up the two kinds of randomness. This generalizes to all printmakers, which would need random selection, and it backs off from cause, which random assignment does allow.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: Seismologists randomly selected 300 buildings from all registered buildings in one city. After a moderate earthquake, they recorded whether each building had been retrofitted for earthquakes. Retrofitted buildings had much less structural damage than buildings that had not been retrofitted.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Retrofitting is associated with less earthquake damage for buildings in that city.
Retrofitting causes less earthquake damage for buildings in that city.
Retrofitting is associated with less earthquake damage for buildings in every city.
Retrofitting is not related to earthquake damage for buildings in that city.
items.explanation: First, ask whether anything was randomly assigned. It wasn't: the seismologists didn't decide which buildings got retrofitted. They only recorded what had already been done. So this is an observational study, and it supports an association, not a cause. Second, ask whether the buildings were randomly selected. They were, from all registered buildings in that one city. So the result can be generalized to buildings in that city, but no further. Choice A is the only one that gets both parts right.

C.why: You got the association right, but you generalized too far. The random sample came from one city's buildings, so the conclusion only covers that city. Other cities may have different soil, building codes and construction methods.

D.why: You assumed that because there was no random assignment, the study shows no relationship at all. Without random assignment you can't claim a cause, but you can still describe the association the data clearly show.

items.stimulus: A city planning office recruited 80 volunteer neighborhood blocks. The office randomly assigned 40 of the blocks to have street trees planted and left the other 40 unchanged. Two summers later, the blocks with new trees had lower average midday street temperatures.

items.stimulus: A textile historian examined 60 nineteenth-century garments that families had donated to a small museum. For each garment, the historian recorded whether it had been stored in acid-free tissue paper before donation and measured how much its dye had faded. Garments that had been stored in acid-free tissue paper showed much less fading, on average, than the others.
items.stem: Based on the design and results of the study, which of the following is an appropriate conclusion?
choices: Storage in acid-free tissue paper caused less fading for the 60 garments studied.
Storage in acid-free tissue paper is associated with less fading for the 60 garments studied.
Storage in acid-free tissue paper is associated with less fading for all nineteenth-century garments.
Storage in acid-free tissue paper causes less fading for all nineteenth-century garments.
items.explanation: The historian only recorded how the families had already stored the garments, so this is an observational study and supports an association, not a cause. The garments were donations, not a random selection, so the finding applies only to the 60 garments studied.

A.why: You accepted a causal claim because the difference in fading was large. Storage was not randomly assigned. For example, families who used acid-free tissue may also have kept their garments away from light.

C.why: You were right to say association, but you generalized from donated garments to all nineteenth-century garments. That would require random selection, and these garments weren't randomly selected.

D.why: This choice needs both kinds of randomness, and the study had neither. Storage wasn't randomly assigned, so you can't claim cause. The garments weren't randomly selected, so you can't generalize beyond them.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: A materials engineer randomly selected 80 steel rods from a production lot of 4,000 rods. Half of the 80 rods were randomly assigned to receive a new zinc-based coating, and the other half were left uncoated. After 30 days in a salt-spray chamber, the coated rods had lost significantly less mass to corrosion than the uncoated rods.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The coating is associated with less corrosion for rods in the lot, but it cannot be shown to cause less corrosion.
The coating causes less corrosion for rods in the production lot of 4,000 rods.
The coating causes less corrosion for steel rods made by any manufacturer.
The coating causes less corrosion, but only for the 80 rods that were tested.
items.explanation: Check both kinds of randomness. The rods were randomly assigned to coated or uncoated, so you can claim that the coating causes the difference. The 80 rods were also randomly selected from the lot of 4,000, so you can extend the conclusion to that whole lot. Choice B gets both parts right.

A.why: You missed that the rods were randomly assigned to the coating. Random assignment is exactly what allows a cause-and-effect claim, so saying only "associated" undersells the evidence.

C.why: You got the causal part right, but the rods came only from this one production lot. Random selection lets you generalize to that lot, not to rods from every manufacturer.

D.why: You ignored the random selection. Because the 80 rods were chosen at random from the lot, the result extends to all 4,000 rods, not only the ones tested.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: A climatologist randomly selected 150 weather stations from a national network of 2,000 stations. For each selected station, she recorded whether it was within 500 meters of a large paved area and its average overnight low temperature for July. Stations near large paved areas had significantly higher average overnight lows than the other stations.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Being near a large paved area causes higher overnight lows at stations in the national network.
Being near a large paved area is associated with higher overnight lows at stations in the national network.
Being near a large paved area is associated with higher overnight lows at weather stations worldwide.
Being near a large paved area causes higher overnight lows, but only at the 150 sampled stations.
items.explanation: The climatologist only recorded where stations already were. Nothing was randomly assigned, so this is an observational study and supports only an association. The 150 stations were randomly selected from the national network of 2,000, so the association can be extended to that network. Choice B gets both parts right.

A.why: This is the trap. The difference is large, but no station was randomly assigned to be near pavement. Without random assignment you can't claim a cause, however strong the association looks.

C.why: You got "associated" right but stretched the population. The stations were sampled from one national network, so the conclusion can't extend to stations around the world.

D.why: You made two errors. You claimed a cause from an observational study, and you ignored that random selection lets the result extend to the whole network of 2,000 stations.

items.subtype_name: Cause and effect or just association
items.stimulus: At one clinic, 120 adults volunteered for a vaccine trial. Each volunteer was randomly assigned to receive either a vaccine made with a new adjuvant or the standard vaccine. Four weeks later, the group that received the new-adjuvant vaccine had significantly higher average antibody levels than the standard group.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The new-adjuvant vaccine causes higher antibody levels among adults across the country.
The new-adjuvant vaccine causes higher antibody levels among people similar to the volunteers.
The new-adjuvant vaccine is associated with higher antibody levels but cannot be shown to cause them.
The new-adjuvant vaccine is associated with higher antibody levels among adults across the country.
items.explanation: The volunteers were randomly assigned to the two vaccines, so you can claim the new adjuvant causes the higher antibody levels. They were not randomly selected from any population, because they chose to volunteer at one clinic. That means the conclusion reaches only people similar to the volunteers. Choice B gets both parts right.

A.why: The causal part is right, but the volunteers weren't randomly selected from all adults in the country. Without random selection you can't generalize to that population.

C.why: This is the trap of mixing up the two kinds of randomness. A missing random sample limits who the result applies to. It doesn't block a causal claim, because random assignment is what permits cause, and this study used random assignment.

D.why: You made two errors. You settled for "associated" even though the treatments were randomly assigned, and you extended the result to the whole country without a random sample.
